rendering.persona_description: Ignacio is a 52-year-old logistics manager for a regional trucking company, married for twenty-six years with two grown kids, one still in college. He coaches a youth baseball team on weekends and prides himself on being the guy people call when something needs fixing. He reads a lot about how things work — engines, contracts, tax law — and likes having an answer for everything, which makes it especially irritating when his own head won't cooperate.
rendering.clinical_context: Ignacio has had chronic, free-floating worry for at least fifteen years — money, his kids, his health, whether the warehouse roof will hold up in a storm — that his doctor and now a therapist call generalized anxiety disorder. He started exposure-based treatment about ten weeks ago, doing structured worry exposure where he sits with uncertain scenarios instead of trying to solve or avoid them, after a stretch of bad insomnia and a scare with his blood pressure pushed him to finally go. He's kept going to sessions but has started telling his wife he thinks he's done, that it isn't doing anything he couldn't do on his own.
rendering.behavioral_description: Ignacio talks in short, declarative sentences and gets prickly fast if he feels like he's being handled or given a script to follow. He'll ask a question and then argue with the answer, testing it, poking holes, more comfortable being unconvinced than agreeing too quickly. He brings up the therapy unprompted just to gripe about it, but pushes back hard if anyone suggests he should stick with it or do it differently, and he deflects with dry humor when a topic gets too close to how scared he actually is.
